title: Ecclesiastes 1:12–18
context: The Preacher introduces himself as having been king over Israel in Jerusalem and describes his project: to search out by wisdom all that is done under the sky. He finds it a heavy burden God has given to humanity, sees everything as vanity and a chasing after wind, and concludes that the crooked cannot be made straight. Having gained great wisdom, he sets his heart to know wisdom and also madness and folly, and finds that increased wisdom brings increased grief. The phrase under the sun, used throughout the book, frames the inquiry as a look at life as it is observed in this world.

verses.text: I, the Preacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher says he was king over Israel in Jerusalem. Arminian readers note that this claim is often linked to Solomon, though others read it as a literary persona; the passage leaves the question open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the past tense, was king, has been read in different ways, and they do not build an argument on it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as establishing the speaker’s royal standing and resources for his inquiry.

verses.text: I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom concerning all that is done under the sky. It is a heavy burden that God has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with.
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher applied his heart to search out by wisdom all that is done, and calls it a heavy burden God has given. Arminian readers note that the search for understanding is itself part of the human calling, though it can be wearying.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the burden as part of life in a world where God has set limits on human understanding. Both traditions read the verse as acknowledging God’s place in the human condition, even when that condition is hard.

verses.text: I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and behold, all is vanity and a chasing after wind.
verses.arminianNotes: He has seen all works done under the sun, and all is vanity and a chasing after wind. Arminian readers note that “chasing after wind” pictures effort spent on something that cannot be grasped or held.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase as pairing with vanity to describe the elusiveness of lasting gain in this world. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the Preacher’s verdict on human works viewed under the sun.

verses.text: That which is crooked can’t be made straight; and that which is lacking can’t be counted.
verses.arminianNotes: What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be counted. Arminian readers see a proverb about the limits of human ability to fix the world’s flaws by effort alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the later echo in Ecclesiastes 7:13, which links crookedness to the work of God. Both traditions read the saying as humbling human pretensions to master life, without turning it into fatalism.

verses.text: I said to myself, “Behold, I have obtained for myself great wisdom above all who were before me in Jerusalem. Yes, my heart has had great experience of wisdom and knowledge.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher says he gained great wisdom above all before him in Jerusalem. Arminian readers note the claim recalls the accounts of Solomon’s wisdom in 1 Kings 3–4, though the book does not name him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the claim as establishing that the Preacher’s conclusions come from one with every advantage of learning. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as setting up a test of wisdom by one well equipped to make it.

verses.text: I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also was a chasing after wind.
verses.arminianNotes: He set his heart to know wisdom and also madness and folly, and found this too a chasing after wind. Arminian readers note that the inquiry includes study of folly in order to understand wisdom more fully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the result as showing that even the fullest study cannot master life’s meaning under the sun. Both traditions read the verse as part of the Preacher’s honest account of the limits of his search.

verses.text: For in much wisdom is much grief; and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.
verses.arminianNotes: In much wisdom is much grief, and increasing knowledge increases sorrow. Arminian readers note that deeper understanding can make one more aware of suffering and injustice in the world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the proverb as a candid word that wisdom alone does not bring happiness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honest about the costs of knowledge, without rejecting wisdom, which the book later commends (2:13).
